abstract: For over 50 years, the database community has developed a wide range of successful engines to answer two fundamental questions: how can database systems run faster, and how can we ensure their correctness? Experience with these engines shows that performance depends on hardware and workloads. As both change over time, we repeatedly redesign and rebuild database systems, a time-consuming and expensive process. Correctness remains another long-standing challenge: recent studies continue to uncover wrong-answer bugs even in mature database engines, despite years of development and testing. To address these, we present GenDB-V, a system that enables AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized to hardware and workloads for performance, and formally verified for correctness. GenDB-V supports specialized implementations of SQL templates and general-purpose engines that accept any query within a supported SQL subset. First, we develop SQLSpec to formalize SQL semantics and deterministically construct fixed, implementation-agnostic synthesis targets for storage preservation and query correctness. Second, we enable joint synthesis of fast code and formal proofs through storage–execution co-optimization, performance-first exploration, and three-layer modular proofs that bridge low-level execution to SQLSpec semantics. Third, we verify the synthesized code and proofs against the fixed synthesis targets in an isolated pipeline, proving SQL correctness and program safety. We evaluate GenDB-V on TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR, a benchmark designed to reduce LLM training-data leakage. For verified template implementations, GenDB-V achieves geometric-mean speedups of 22.0–61.3$\times$ over DuckDB and Umbra. For a verified general-purpose engine, GenDB-V also achieves speedups of 1.27–3.4$\times$ on TPC-H. GenDB-V also achieves better performance than a testing-based LLM synthesis method, while our audit and tests expose incorrect answers in that method’s implementations for 16 of 28 templates. This project is available at https://github.com/GenLang-V/GenDB-V.

sections.body: The introduction argues that database performance depends on hardware and workloads, so engines are repeatedly redesigned. Testing keeps finding bugs: EET found 35 logic bugs across five database systems, and SQLancer++ reported 196 bugs across 18 systems. Formal verification covers every input in its proof, but verifying seL4's 8,700-line C kernel required approximately 20 person-years. The paper proposes GenDB-V, which has AI agents synthesize engines using SQLSpec targets, joint code and proof synthesis, and an isolated Verus pipeline. Reported results are geometric-mean speedups of 22.0–61.3× over DuckDB and Umbra for template implementations, and 1.27–3.4× for the general engine on TPC-H.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Database engines need costly rebuilds and testing still misses bugs, so GenDB-V has AI agents synthesize engines verified for correctness.

sections.body: GenDB-V has three stages. Deterministic target construction translates the input SQL, schema, and integrity constraints into fixed formal targets using SQLSpec, a formal library in Verus based on PostgreSQL documentation. Joint code and proof synthesis then lets agents co-design storage and execution and write proofs in three layers. Independent verification checks the generated code and proofs against the fixed targets, and on failure returns feedback to the agent. The trusted foundation is SQLSpec, target construction, the verifier, the compiler, and the runtime environment. No agent-generated code or proof is trusted. The Rust compiler erases proof code, so query execution has no proof-checking overhead.
sections.heading: GenDB-V Overview
sections.headline: GenDB-V separates correctness targets from agent search, and an independent verifier admits only code that meets the fixed targets.

sections.body: SQLSpec defines SQL semantics for a core analytical subset covering the features needed by TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR, summarized in Table 1. It models nulls, duplicate rows, runtime SQL errors, and row order, and it rejects unsupported features such as window functions and recursive queries. Permitted outcomes include every ordering that follows ORDER BY keys, so valid execution plans are not rejected. A verified reference interpreter, validated against PostgreSQL, is the initial baseline for engine synthesis. For each SQL template, a deterministic translator builds a target that requires execution to return a permitted outcome on every valid database and every allowed parameter binding. Storage builders must preserve all input data without loss.
sections.heading: Formal Synthesis Targets
sections.headline: SQLSpec formalizes SQL semantics so fixed synthesis targets can be built deterministically from each SQL workload, outside agent control.

sections.body: Joint synthesis addresses three difficulties: storage and execution jointly determine speed, proofs are expensive to write, and a single monolithic proof is too large to check. Agents may choose custom storage under a storage policy, and they must state physical invariants in the representation predicate that execution proofs use. Agents first prototype designs in an unverified diagnostic mode (`--no-verify`), then write proofs only for the fastest design. The proof has three layers: storage reader contracts, physical loop invariants, and inductive bridge lemmas that connect execution to SQLSpec semantics. In the count example, `count_above` is verified with a loop invariant, and `bridge_count` links its result to the specification.
sections.heading: Joint Code and Proof Synthesis
sections.headline: Agents co-optimize storage and execution, prototype without proofs, then prove only the fastest design through three modular proof layers.

sections.body: Verification runs in an isolated environment. SQLSpec, the schema constraints, the parameter domains, and the storage specification are read-only, as is a top-level entry point that enforces the fixed target as its postcondition. Verus, which uses the Z3 solver, checks each function's contracts. Unsafe features such as unsafe pointers and external libraries are rejected, and assume and admit are disabled. A single `--compile` pass verifies and compiles the code into a shared library, so the binary matches the verified source. Verus checks a strictly decreasing measure on every loop and recursive function, which guarantees termination. Limits: proofs cover only databases that satisfy the declared constraints, and termination assumes sufficient memory and stack space and no indefinite starvation of runnable threads.
sections.heading: Independent Verification
sections.headline: An isolated Verus pipeline with read-only specifications checks agent proofs and compiles the verified code into a shared library.

sections.body: Experiments use a server with two 16-core Intel Xeon Gold 5218 processors and 384 GB of RAM, with Claude Opus 5.5 for both GenDB-V and the LLM-based baseline. Workloads are all 22 TPC-H templates at scale factor 100 and all 6 SEC-EDGAR templates at scale factor 3, each averaged over three parameter bindings. Baselines are DuckDB 1.5.6 and Umbra 26.08. Storage is capped at the uncompressed source-file size. Table 2 reports TPC-H workload time at 1 thread: DuckDB 367.841 s, Umbra 170.103 s, plain arrays 50.134 s, and joint optimization 10.380 s. Speedups are reported as geometric means across templates and thread counts.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Verified template implementations reach geometric-mean speedups of 22.0–61.3× over DuckDB and Umbra across TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR.

sections.body: Prior LLM-based SQL synthesis, including CodexDB, GenesisDB, GenDB, and Bespoke OLAP, targets customizable code or performance, and checks correctness by testing against a reference system. The audit and tests of Bespoke OLAP exposed incorrect answers for 16 of 28 templates. JetStream is concurrent work that synthesizes query-specific accelerators, including a formally verified stateful variant. GenDB-V differs in that SQLSpec models nullable inputs, three-valued logic, and SQL-error outcomes, which JetStream does not. GenDB-V can also verify a general-purpose engine, while JetStream supports only SQL templates. JetStream reports a 2.1× geometric-mean speedup over DuckDB for its stateless accelerators. Earlier formal SQL work mainly verified query rewrites.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior LLM synthesis checks correctness by testing, while concurrent JetStream includes a formally verified stateful variant.

sections.body: GenDB-V enables AI agents to synthesize formally verified SQL template implementations and general-purpose database engines. Fixed formal synthesis targets and independent verification let agents jointly explore storage designs, execution code, and proofs. The experimental results show that formal correctness can accompany substantial speedups over established engines. The conclusion presents this as a promising path toward AI-generated and formally verified database systems.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Formal correctness and substantial speedups over established engines together suggest a path toward AI-generated verified database systems.
